## Agenda {.toc}

1. Why classical methods fall short on administrative trajectories
2. The key idea — treat sequences of events as text
3. Three model architectures, in plain terms
4. Result I — student enrollment pathways (3 million students)
5. Result II — medical care trajectories (70 million patients)
6. A new analytical infrastructure for NSIs

# The Problem {.section}

## Millions of individual trajectories, one hard problem

Administrative registers now record every categorical event in millions of lives.

::: {.col-left}
**What the data look like**

```
Student A:   L1-Maths → L2-Maths → L3-Maths → M1-Maths
Student B:   L1-Law   → L2-Law   → re-L1-Law → dropout
Patient C:   GP visit → Medication → Hospital
             Jan 2016    Mar 2016     Jun 2016
Patient D:   Screening → Diagnosis → Chemo → Chemo → …
```

Individual = **a sequence of categorical events** over time.

Vocabulary: 940 course-types · 7,204 medical codes
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Three challenges — all at once**

**① High cardinality**
Thousands of event types → transition matrices become intractable,
feature spaces explode.

**② Long-range dependence**
An event at step 1 shapes outcomes at step 10.
Markov models cannot capture this.

**③ Irregular timing**
Events happen at individual-driven intervals.
Fixed-period panel models are not designed for this.
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
Each challenge has been addressed in isolation. **No existing framework handles all three jointly.** Language model architectures can.
:::

# The Key Idea {.section}

## Trajectories are sentences — events are words

::: {.col-left}
**NLP solved this for text**

A sentence = sequence of tokens drawn from a large vocabulary.

Language models learn, directly from data:
- how words relate (even with 100 000+ distinct words)
- how context accumulates over long distances
- how meaning is shaped by position and timing

**No manual feature engineering. No transition matrix.**
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Our translation**

| NLP concept | Panel data equivalent |
|---|---|
| Word | Event type (course, medical code…) |
| Sentence | Individual trajectory |
| Vocabulary | Set of all possible event types |
| Next-word prediction | Next-event prediction |
| Sentence embedding | Trajectory summary vector |

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
Train a language model on administrative trajectories.
It learns how events relate, how histories unfold, and — with one extension — how irregular time flows.
:::

# Three Architectures {.section}

## Ingredient 1 — Token embeddings: discrete → geometry

Every event type is mapped to a dense, learnable vector.

```
  "L1-Maths"    →  [ 0.31, −0.12,  0.74, … ]  ∈ ℝ^d
  "L2-Maths"    →  [ 0.29, −0.10,  0.71, … ]  ← close: students move between them
  "L1-Law"      →  [−0.55,  0.43, −0.20, … ]  ← far: rarely taken in sequence
  "Cardiology"  →  [ 0.11,  0.88, −0.34, … ]
```

- **One-hot encoding** gives every event its own independent axis — no notion of similarity.
- **Learned embeddings** place events that co-occur in trajectories close together, automatically.
- Works for any vocabulary size. No transition matrix needed.

::: {.highlight-box}
The embedding matrix is the first layer in every model below. The architectures differ in *how they process the sequence* once events are embedded.
:::

## Ingredient 2 — Sequential vs. parallel processing

::: {.col-left}
**RNNs (GRU / LSTM) — rolling memory**

```
Event 1 → Event 2 → Event 3 → predict?
  [h₁] ──→ [h₂] ──→  [h₃]  ──→  output
```

At each step: compress all past history into a single hidden state **h**.

**✓** Natural, chronological flow — lightweight on short sequences

**✗** Early events fade from memory · No parallelisation
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Transformers — attention over full history**

```
Event 1  ─┐
Event 2  ─┼──→  every event attends to all past events  ──→  output
Event 3  ─┘       (in a single parallel pass)
```

At each position: compute a relevance score to every prior event, update the representation as a weighted average.

**✓** Perfect long-range memory · Full parallelisation

**✗** Needs more data · Slower on very short sequences
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
**Rule of thumb used in this paper:** short, regular sequences (≤ 8 steps) → GRU.
Large-scale, irregular, long sequences → Transformer.
:::

## Ingredient 3 — Adding continuous time

Standard models treat all steps as equally spaced. **Medical data are not.**

::: {.col-left}
**Two additions**

**① Time embeddings (Time2Vec)**
The timestamp of each event is encoded as a learned vector
added to the token embedding.
→ The model knows *when* an event happened, not only *what*.

**② Joint time prediction (Delphi loss)**
At each step, predict both:
- the **type** of the next event (cross-entropy)
- the **expected waiting time** (exponential likelihood)

The predicted delay is driven by the full trajectory history at that point.
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Why it matters**

```
Patient A:  Heart failure → [3 days]  → Cardiology
Patient B:  Heart failure → [6 months] → Cardiology
```

Same events. Very different clinical stories.

The time gap *is* information.
The model learns to predict shorter waits after acute events.

Before calibration: model overestimates short delays.
After **temperature scaling**: predicted and observed means align.
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

# Result I — Student Pathways {.section}

## 3 million students, 940 course-types, one GRU

::: {.col-left}
**Data**

- ~3 million students, *baccalauréat* cohorts 2017–2022
- ~10 million enrollment records
- Vocabulary: **940 course-types** (L1 bachelor → PhD)
- Sequence length: up to **8** (one per academic year)
- Covariates: gender, age, bac grade & specialty, parental SPC, school Social Positioning Index, geographic origin
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Model**

- **GRU** — right fit for short, regular sequences
- ~3 million parameters
- Covariates embedded and summed to initialise the hidden state
- Standard cross-entropy loss (yearly gaps are constant — no time extension needed)
- Best model selected on 500k held-out students
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
At this scale and vocabulary size (940 classes), standard regression, ensemble, and boosting methods were **not trainable**. Sequence models are the only viable option.
:::

## Going beyond inertia

**Baseline:** a bigram that predicts the next enrollment from the current one only.
No covariates, no history. A direct measure of how much *inertia* explains.

| Model | Top-1 | Top-3 | Top-5 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Bigram — inertia only | 62.3 % | 79.7 % | 83.9 % |
| GRU | **66.7 %** | **82.8 %** | **86.6 %** |

*(Accuracy on the test set of 600k students, excluding the first enrollment which the bigram cannot predict.)*

::: {.highlight-box}
Most students continue on the same track — inertia is already a strong signal. The GRU improves by combining **full trajectory history** with **covariate information** (parental background, school SPI…).

This makes the model directly policy-relevant: we can estimate the marginal effect of social background on transition probabilities — and the hidden states **h** are compact trajectory embeddings ready for clustering, matching, and typology construction.
:::

# Result II — Medical Pathways {.section}

## The entire French population's health history

::: {.col-left}
**Data — SNDS (National Health Database)**

- **70 million** patients covered
- **8 billion** medical events
- **7,204 token** vocabulary:

| Event family | Tokens |
|---|:-:|
| Specialty consultations | 83 |
| Clinical procedures (CCAM) | 936 |
| Medications (ATC) | 704 |
| Hospital diagnoses (ICD-10) | 3 275 |
| Admissions, emergencies, deaths | — |

- Irregular timestamps: multiple events per day possible, or none for months
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Model**

- **Transformer** — right fit for large scale + irregular time
- Time-aware: Time2Vec embeddings + Delphi loss
- Jointly predicts at each step:
  - **Type** of the next medical event
  - **Expected waiting time** until it occurs
- Gender and birth year prepended as context

**Scale check**

Validation loss drops sharply with both model size and training set size, before reaching a plateau — confirming the dataset saturates this architecture rather than the reverse.
:::

## The model discovers the map of medicine — unsupervised

The Transformer learns a 256-dimensional vector for each of the 7,204 medical tokens,
**with no clinical labels**. Projecting to 2D (UMAP):

```
  [Obstetrics] · · [Senology]
       ·                ·
  [Gynecology]      [Oncology] · ·
                           ·
  [Ophthalmology]   [Emergency] · [Trauma codes]
        · ·
  [Urology] · · ·   [Cardiology] · · ·
                ·
  [Dentistry]     [Psychiatry]
```

- **Clinically coherent clusters** form purely from trajectory co-occurrence
- **Higher-order structure** is preserved: gynecology sits adjacent to senology;
  emergency neighbors trauma codes
- The model has internalized the **logic of care pathways**, not merely memorized token pairs

::: {.highlight-box}
This structured geometry emerges without any supervision — it is entirely a product of learning to predict the next event in 8 billion medical records.
:::

## Zero-shot predictions rival supervised models

**Task (unseen during training):** given a random point in a patient's trajectory, predict whether a specific event occurs within 30 / 180 / 365 days.

::: {.col-left}
**Three approaches compared**

- **Naïve baseline:** logistic regression on age and gender only
- **Logistic on embeddings:** trained on **100k** patients
- **Zero-shot:** model's output logits, no additional training at all

Evaluated on **1 million** held-out patients.
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Results**

Zero-shot is **competitive with the supervised approach** trained on 100k patients.

Large gains for history-driven events:
dialysis, chemotherapy → model captures the clinical logic.

Modest but consistent gains for unpredictable events:
emergency presentations → even here, history adds signal.
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
The model has learned a **transferable encoding of medical history**.
It generalises to tasks it was never trained on — with **no labelled data required**.
:::

# A New Infrastructure for NSIs {.section}

## More than a predictor — a reusable analytical backbone

::: {.col-left}
**What we have shown**

✓ Sequence models handle high cardinality, long-range dependence, and irregular timing **jointly** — no classical method does

✓ Trained on raw administrative data, they learn **structured, semantically meaningful representations** of individual histories

✓ These representations **transfer to downstream tasks unseen during training**, without retraining
:::

::: {.col-right}
**The institutional opportunity**

One model, pre-trained on a national register, serves as a **shared backbone**:

- Policy evaluation and associative studies
- Subgroup characterisation and matching
- Control variables for causal inference
- *(Future work)* Privacy-preserving synthetic trajectory generation

**One model. Many research questions. Lower barrier to entry for every team.**
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
**Governance is not optional.** Pre-trained pathway models need the same standards as official statistics: documented training data, versioning, auditability, and strict access controls on individual-level embeddings — before any dissemination.
:::

## What to bring back from this talk

| Challenge | Our answer |
|---|---|
| High-cardinality categorical states | Token embeddings — learned geometry, no manual mapping |
| Long-range path dependence | Transformers — direct attention across the full history |
| Irregular event timing | Time2Vec + Delphi loss — continuous time baked into training |
| Scalability | Trained end-to-end on billions of raw records, no feature engineering |
| Reusability across research teams | Pre-trained pathway model as shared NSI infrastructure |

::: {.highlight-box}
**The shift:** from one model per research question, to one pre-trained model serving many — the same transition NLP made a decade ago, now applied to the structured administrative data NSIs already hold at scale.
:::
